scenes.tts: For most of the last century, the rule was that the neurons you are born with are the neurons you keep. Adult rodents break that rule. All their lives they make new neurons in two places. One is a thin layer in the wall of the lateral ventricles, the subventricular zone. Its young neurons travel forward to the olfactory bulb. The other is the dentate gyrus of the hippocampus. In both places, the new neurons join working circuits.
scenes.visual: A side view of a mouse brain. The rule appears as a crossed-out caption. Two spots light up: the ventricle wall, with a chain of young neurons streaming forward to the olfactory bulb, and the dentate gyrus arc in the hippocampus, with new dots appearing in it.

scenes.tts: Which cell makes them? In mice, a drug killed the fast-dividing cells of the subventricular zone. Cells that look like astrocytes survived. They began dividing and rebuilt the zone. So the stem cell is astrocyte-like. It makes fast-dividing precursors, which make young neurons that migrate. The dentate gyrus has stem cells like these too.
scenes.visual: The SVZ lineage drawn as B, C and A cells beside the ventricle. The drug wipes out C and A cells; the star-shaped B cells remain, divide, and the C and A cells return. Then the arrow B to C to A to olfactory bulb interneuron.

scenes.tts: How can anyone tell that a neuron is new? Give a labelled DNA building block. Only cells copying their DNA build it in. A neuron that has stopped dividing normally does not copy its DNA again. So a labelled neuron found weeks later most likely came from a cell that divided after the dose. A second stain shows that the labelled cell is a neuron.
scenes.visual: A dividing cell takes in a glowing label; a resting neuron beside it does not. Weeks later, a neuron with a glowing nucleus, and a second colour marking it as a neuron.

scenes.tts: A new neuron matters only if it is wired in. Over several weeks, new granule neurons grow dendrites and send axons into the hippocampal circuit. In adult canaries, new neurons in a song nucleus were found to respond to sound.
scenes.visual: A young granule neuron in the dentate gyrus grows dendrites outward and an axon toward the next hippocampal region, over a ticking week counter with no numbers. Cut to a canary singing and a new neuron flashing to a sound wave.

scenes.tts: What are they for? In mice, young dentate neurons are thought to help with pattern separation, telling apart similar places or events. Mice in which adult neurogenesis was blocked did worse at telling apart nearby locations. In the olfactory bulb, new interneurons have been linked to odour learning. Signals in the niche and experience set the output. Mice with a running wheel had more new dentate neurons.
scenes.visual: Two nearly identical rooms side by side, then two far apart; a mouse picks correctly. Cut to the olfactory bulb with new interneurons and an odour cloud. End on a mouse on a running wheel and the dentate arc filling with more new dots.

scenes.tts: What about people? Bomb tests in the nineteen fifties and early sixties put extra carbon fourteen into the air, and into the DNA of cells made then. Neurons at the back of the cortex, and in the olfactory bulb, are as old as the person. Some hippocampal neurons are younger. Stains for young neurons disagree, partly because the stain fades after death. Recent reviews read the evidence as favouring some new neurons in the adult human hippocampus, from several methods. How many, and what they do, is still open.
scenes.visual: A rise-and-fall curve of carbon-14 in the air, a dividing cell's DNA filling to that year's level. A human brain: cortex and olfactory bulb tagged with the birth year, the hippocampus with a few later tags. Two stained panels, one fading. End on the hippocampus with an open question mark.
